:::: {.concept-card key="absolute-integrability" tags="mathematics"}
## absolute integrability

A random quantity is absolutely integrable when its expected absolute value is finite.
This guarantees that its expectation is a finite number.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="affine-map" tags="mathematics"}
## affine map

A transformation consisting of a linear map followed by a translation.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="automatic-differentiation" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## automatic differentiation

Computing derivatives of a program by combining the derivative rules of its elementary operations through the chain rule.
Operations such as stop-gradient can intentionally define special differentiation behaviour.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="chain-rule" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## chain rule

The rule for differentiating a composition of functions by multiplying the appropriate local derivatives or Jacobians.
Contributions are added when several graph paths connect an input to an output.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="conditional-distribution" tags="mathematics"}
## conditional distribution

A distribution describing a random quantity given specified information, on conditioning events or values for which it is defined.
It may retain uncertainty or assign all probability to a single outcome.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="conditional-expectation" tags="mathematics"}
## conditional expectation

The average of a random quantity under the distribution remaining after specified information is given.
With squared-error loss and finite second moments, it is the best unrestricted predictor from that information.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="confidence-score" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## confidence score

A numerical score used to rank or select a model prediction.
Its interpretation as a probability requires additional assumptions or calibration.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="convex-function" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## convex function

A function on a convex domain whose value at a weighted average of two inputs is no greater than the same weighted average of their function values.
Its graph lies below the line segment joining any two points on the graph.

::: {.concept-prompt}
State the definition, including the condition on the domain and the quantifiers.
:::

::: {.concept-statement}
Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be convex. A function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is **convex** if, for every $x,y\in C$ and every $t\in[0,1]$,

$$
f(tx+(1-t)y)\leq t f(x)+(1-t)f(y).
$$

The graph lies at or below each chord joining two of its points.
The domain condition ensures that $tx+(1-t)y$ belongs to $C$.
:::
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="cosine-similarity" tags="mathematics"}
## cosine similarity

The dot product of two nonzero vectors divided by the product of their Euclidean lengths.
It compares directions rather than vector magnitudes.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="differentiable-function" tags="mathematics"}
## differentiable function

A function that admits a linear approximation near the point being considered, with an error that becomes negligible relative to the input change.
In one dimension, the slope of that approximation is the derivative.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="euclidean-norm" tags="mathematics"}
## euclidean norm

The square root of the sum of squared magnitudes of a vector’s coordinates.
It is the usual vector length in the specified coordinates.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="gaussian-distribution" tags="mathematics"}
## gaussian distribution

A probability distribution specified by a mean and covariance; in one dimension with positive variance its density is bell-shaped.
A standard multivariate Gaussian has zero mean and identity covariance.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="geometric-decay" tags="mathematics"}
## geometric decay

A sequence of nonnegative weights in which each successive weight is multiplied by the same factor smaller than one.
In an EMA, this factor determines how quickly older observations lose weight.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="gradient-ascent" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## gradient ascent

An iterative optimisation method that moves parameters or inputs in the direction of a function’s gradient to increase its value locally.
The step size determines how far each update moves.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="independent-samples" tags="mathematics"}
## independent samples

Random samples whose joint distribution factors into the product of their individual distributions.
Independence alone does not say that they have the same distribution.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="latent-variable" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## latent variable

A variable included in a model but not directly observed in the example being explained.
Its coordinates need not correspond to identifiable physical causes.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="marginal-distribution" tags="mathematics"}
## marginal distribution

The distribution of selected variables obtained from a joint distribution by summing or integrating over the other variables.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="marginalisation" tags="mathematics"}
## marginalisation

Summing or integrating a joint distribution over variables that are not retained.
The result describes the remaining variables while accounting for the possible values of the removed variables.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="matrix-exponential" tags="mathematics"}
## matrix exponential

The matrix function defined by the power series I + A + A squared divided by 2 factorial, and so on.
It propagates a constant-coefficient homogeneous linear differential equation.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="measurable-function" tags="mathematics"}
## measurable function

A function whose preimage of every measurable output set is a measurable input event.
This lets a probability model assign probabilities consistently to events defined through the function.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="nat" tags="mathematics"}
## nat

The unit of information obtained when logarithms use base e.
Changing the logarithm base changes the unit and rescales the numerical information value.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="normalising-constant" tags="mathematics"}
## normalising constant

A sum or integral of unnormalised weights used to make their total probability equal one.
It must be positive and finite for the resulting distribution to be well defined.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="posterior" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## posterior distribution

The conditional distribution of unknown parameters or latent variables after incorporating specified observations under a model.
It combines the likelihood of those observations with the prior.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="prior" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## prior distribution

A distribution specified before incorporating the observation currently being explained.
It may describe parameters or latent variables and may already condition on other supplied context.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="probability-mass-function" tags="mathematics"}
## probability mass function

A function assigning the probability of each value of a discrete random variable.
Its values are nonnegative and sum to one.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="quantile" tags="mathematics"}
## quantile

A threshold associated with a chosen cumulative probability level.
A percentile is a quantile whose level is expressed as a percentage; finite-sample estimation conventions can differ.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="random-variable" tags="mathematics"}
## random variable

A measurable function assigning a value to each outcome of a probability model.
Its distribution describes the probabilities of those values, while a realisation is one value it takes.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="recurrence" tags="computer-software mathematics"}
## recurrence

A rule defining each value of a sequence using earlier values and, when applicable, new inputs.
Initial values are needed to determine the sequence.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="second-moment" tags="mathematics"}
## second moment

The expectation of a squared scalar random variable, or of a squared norm for a random vector.
A finite second moment means that this expectation is finite.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="standard-deviation" tags="mathematics"}
## standard deviation

The nonnegative square root of a variance.
It measures spread in the same units as the random quantity.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="stationary-point" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## stationary point

A point at which a differentiable scalar objective has zero gradient.
It can be a minimum, a maximum, or a point that is neither.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="variance" tags="mathematics"}
## variance

The expected squared deviation of a random quantity from its mean, when this quantity exists.
It measures spread in squared units.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="variational-distribution" tags="machine-learning mathematics"}
## variational distribution

A distribution from a chosen family with adjustable parameters, used to approximate a posterior that is difficult to work with directly.
Optimising its parameters does not guarantee equality with the true posterior.
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="subgradient" tags="mathematics"}
## subgradient and subdifferential

::: {.concept-prompt}
Define a subgradient of a convex function at a point. How does it differ from the subdifferential?
:::

::: {.concept-statement}
For a convex function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, a vector $g\in\mathbb R^d$ is a **subgradient at $x\in C$** if

$$
f(z)\geq f(x)+g^\top(z-x)\qquad\text{for every }z\in C.
$$

The **subdifferential** $\partial f(x)$ is the set of all such vectors $g$.
The inequality is global over $C$; it describes an affine supporting function.
:::
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="finite-expectation" tags="mathematics"}
## finite expectation

::: {.concept-prompt}
Define the expectation of a real random variable, and state a condition that makes it finite.
:::

::: {.concept-statement}
For a real random variable $X$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, if $\mathbb E[|X|]<\infty$, its finite **expectation** is

$$
\mathbb E[X]=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,dP(\omega).
$$

For a discrete distribution, this is $\sum_x xP(X=x)$; for a distribution with density $p$, it is $\int_{\mathbb R}x p(x)\,dx$.
Absolute integrability excludes an undefined cancellation of positive and negative infinities.
:::
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="linearity-expectation" tags="mathematics"}
## linearity of expectation

::: {.concept-prompt}
State and prove linearity for two real random variables. Is independence required?
:::

::: {.concept-statement}
If $X,Y$ are integrable real random variables on the same probability space and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, then

$$
\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\mathbb E[X]+b\mathbb E[Y].
$$

Independence is not required.
:::

::: {.concept-proof}
The triangle inequality gives $|aX+bY|\leq |a||X|+|b||Y|$, so $aX+bY$ is integrable.
Linearity of the integral then gives

$$
\int_\Omega(aX+bY)\,dP=a\int_\Omega X\,dP+b\int_\Omega Y\,dP.
$$

Both variables are integrated against the same joint probability measure; no factorisation or independence assumption appears.
:::
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="jensen-differentiable" tags="mathematics"}
## Jensen's inequality: differentiable case

::: {.concept-prompt}
State a version for a differentiable convex function and prove it using a supporting tangent line.
:::

::: {.concept-statement}
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable and convex, and let $X\in I$ almost surely.
Assume $X$ and $f(X)$ are integrable and $m=\mathbb E[X]\in I$. Then

$$
f(\mathbb E[X])\leq\mathbb E[f(X)].
$$

This card proves the differentiable case; the general convex form does not require differentiability.
:::

::: {.concept-proof}
For any $x\in I$ and $0<t<1$, convexity gives

$$
\frac{f(m+t(x-m))-f(m)}{t}\leq f(x)-f(m).
$$

Letting $t\downarrow0$ yields $f'(m)(x-m)\leq f(x)-f(m)$.
Thus $f(X)\geq f(m)+f'(m)(X-m)$ almost surely. Taking expectations gives

$$
\mathbb E[f(X)]\geq f(m)+f'(m)(\mathbb E[X]-m)=f(m).
$$
:::
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="absolute-value-subdifferential" tags="mathematics"}
## subdifferential of absolute value at zero

::: {.concept-prompt}
Find $\partial f(0)$ for $f(x)=|x|$, and prove both necessity and sufficiency.
:::

::: {.concept-statement}
For $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=|x|$,

$$
\partial f(0)=[-1,1].
$$

Every number in this interval is a supporting slope at zero.
:::

::: {.concept-proof}
The defining inequality at zero is $|z|\geq gz$ for every $z\in\mathbb R$.
For $z>0$, division by $z$ gives $g\leq1$.
For $z<0$, division reverses the inequality and gives $g\geq-1$.
These conditions are necessary.

Conversely, if $g\in[-1,1]$, then for $z\geq0$, $gz\leq z=|z|$; for $z<0$, $gz\leq-z=|z|$.
The inequality holds everywhere, so these conditions are also sufficient.
:::
::::

:::: {.concept-card key="zero-subgradient" tags="mathematics"}
## zero subgradient and a global minimum

::: {.concept-prompt}
Characterise a global minimiser using the subdifferential. Prove both directions.
:::

::: {.concept-statement}
Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C$, with the subdifferential defined relative to $C$.
For $x_*\in C$,

$$
0\in\partial f(x_*)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(x_*)\leq f(z)\ \text{for all }z\in C.
$$
:::

::: {.concept-proof}
Substitute $g=0$ into the subgradient inequality:
$f(z)\geq f(x_*)+0^\top(z-x_*)=f(x_*)$ for every $z\in C$.
This is exactly the definition of a global minimum, so the same calculation proves both directions.
:::
::::
